newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian wines pour into the United States market.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian wines pour into the United States market.

text.p: The Australian wine industry has launched a new push into the United States which trade officials believe could quadruple sales to more than US$300 million in five years.

In a boom similar to the explosion of interest in Australian wines in Great Britain in the 1980s, exporters have been selling all the wine they can produce for the U.S. market over the last 12 months.

Australian Trade Commission executive general manager Michael Johnson told Reuters the industry was on the edge of its biggest international success after more than a decade of establishing a presence in North America.

Currently Australian wines bring in more than US$75 million from export sales to the United States. Shipments of more than 12 million litres over the last two years are expected to be easily exceeded over the coming 12 months.

"In three years time, mark my words, it will be US$150 million and I think it could make US$200 million and certainly in five years time we must break US$300 million in the U.S.," said Johnson who was a trade representative in London ten years ago when Australian wine suddenly found favour with British drinkers.
"In Britain we had lost our way a bit producing things like "Kanga Rouge" and basically battling great prejudice, but we turned it around targeting the five to eight pound range."
Australian now has a seven per cent market share in Britain, exporting more than 5.5 million cases worth US$320 million annually.

Sales of product from more than 50 Australian wineries gives Australia the fastest growing industry presence in the United States, which is the third largest market and catching up with Italy and France.
The Australian Wine and Brandy Corp is sponsoring a marketing thrust that could make the Australian product as widely available in America as French and Italian wines.
Frank Passanante, Austrade's Commissioner specialising in the food and beverage industry from New York, said Australian wines got a foot firmly in the U.S. cellar door during the 1980's.
"Australia was very fashionable in the U.S. for a time and it heightened awareness, then the exchange rate was very favourable and the wines found a solid market niche," he said.
Most of the large Australian wine companies like Rosemount, BRL Hardy and Southcorp which owns 17 wine brands including Lindemans, Penfolds, Seppelt and Seaview have their products on U.S. shelves.
And Australians travelling in the U.S. are often surprised to find their favourite wines at prices about the same and sometimes less than at home.
"It's the different market pressures that dictates price," said Passanante. "This is an enormously competitive market where Californian wine obviously has a big head start."
Despite the price squeeze, the U.S. is a more profitable market for Australian producers than Britain.

The Australian push in the U.S. in recent years had been stymied by a shortage of quality export product, but winemakers plan to have more than enough to meet demand over the next few years and are looking to take advantage of a downturn in the quantity and quality of Californian and Washington state wine.
Austrade has also stepped up its assistance to the industry, taking control of the generic promotion of Australian wines in the United States.

Southcorp which has 40 per cent of the Australian slice of the U.S. market has also boosted its marketing, buoyed by a series of critical successes, including The Wine Spectator magazine's Wine of the Year Award for Penfold's Grange which will be awarded in San Francisco later this month.
"It is enormously important that we get this sort of recognition through the wine press," said Southcorp vice president of marketing Carl Jaeger.

Southcorp, like most of the major players takes a two pronged approach to the North American market, pushing solid, easy drinking wines like a Lindemans chardonnay at relatively low prices (around $US7) while trading off the rapidly growing reputation of the quality of Australian wines.

"We provide a good seven dollar bottle of wine -- for the consumer it doesn't matter if it's Australian or Californian -- but at the same time there is an increasing awareness of quality Australian wines at the higher end," Jaeger said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
